chapter: Hampton band, Honolulu and the war years
title: Pearl Harbor, driving a cab and the crossing home
summary: After the Pearl Harbor attack he drives a cab, then returns in June 1942 on an Army transport, and briefly tries Chicago.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years

blocks.x: We played there until the bombing of Pearl Harbor.
That was December 7, 1941.
That's correct. They closed all the dancehalls so we were out of work. So most of the musicians got jobs in defense.
In Hawaii?
In Hawaii. So they were told that they couldn't quit until the war was over, but I knew that they were freezing the jobs in
defense, so I got me a job driving a cab.
Driving a cab was not considered defense work?
No. It was my own cab and I wasn't working for anybody, and I could leave anytime.

By June of '42, I had transportation accommodations with permission to leave with my family. After a dangerous crossing of the Pacific on an Army transport ship, with three warships escorting her to protect us from Japanese subs.
Did the government give you permission to come over on that ship?
Oh yes. They gave us notice, they'd give us twenty-four hours notice, to stay by the phone, have money ready for your tickets; that was the order we got, see.
That was quite an experience; that was a very dangerous time,
Yes.
It was funny how the ship had to zig zag to try and duck the submarines.
The Japanese submarines were in the area; is that it?
Yes.
After eight days we arrived in San Francisco. I sent my wife to Los Angeles and I continued on to Chicago because I thought maybe I could go back there and re-settle.
I was there only one week, enough to convince me that Chicago was not the place.
After Hawaii and California, you had to come back?
That's right.
